sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

You'll build a robust personal decision framework for picking the right AI tool for any task — including how to evaluate new tools as they emerge, how to build an optimal multi-tool stack for different budgets, and why tool routing is a skill that improves everything else. This is the synthesis lesson for Part 2.

## The Core Routing Principle

Using the wrong AI tool isn't fatal — most can do most things adequately. But using the *right* tool is noticeably better, faster, and more reliable. The difference between asking a research question in Claude versus Perplexity is the difference between an answer you have to trust blindly and an answer you can verify in 30 seconds.

**Four principles before the framework:**

**1. Don't be loyal to one tool.** The best AI practitioners maintain a small toolkit and route tasks to the right tool. Becoming a one-tool person means missing genuine strengths you're not using.

**2. The right tool is often the one you don't have to leave your workflow to use.** A mediocre tool you can access in 2 seconds beats a great tool that requires switching contexts. Gemini inside Gmail, Copilot in Edge — these win on friction reduction even when they're not the best standalone tool.

**3. Use both and compare when unsure.** If you genuinely can't decide between Claude and ChatGPT for a task, run it in both. Direct comparison is faster and more reliable than any guide.

**4. Your routing will evolve.** This framework is a starting point. As you use these tools more, you'll develop strong personal preferences. Trust your own experience over any recommendation.

## The Decision Framework by Task Type

**"I need real sources and citations."**
→ **Perplexity** for quick cited research; **Perplexity Deep Research** for comprehensive reports. Use when: health questions, current events, fact-checking claims, recent news, anything where the source authority matters as much as the answer.

**"I need to write, analyse, or reason through something complex."**
→ **Claude** as the default. Best instruction-following, best long-form writing, most consistent on complex analytical tasks. Add extended thinking mode for multi-step problems.

**"I need to run Python code on data, or generate images in the same workflow."**
→ **ChatGPT** with Code Interpreter for data analysis; DALL-E 3 for images within the conversation.

**"I have a huge document or need live web search."**
→ **Gemini 2.5 Pro** for 1M-token context (processing very long documents); **Gemini** for live Google Search integration.

**"I'm working inside Gmail, Docs, or Sheets."**
→ **Gemini** — already inside those tools, no tab switching.

**"I'm working inside Outlook, Teams, Word, or Excel."**
→ **Microsoft 365 Copilot** — meets you where your work already lives.

**"I'm reading a web page and want AI alongside it."**
→ **Copilot in Edge** — sidebar reads the page you're on, no copy-paste needed.

**"I need an image, voice, music, or short video."**
→ Specialist tools: Bing Image Creator (free images), ElevenLabs (voice), Suno (music), Runway (video). General chat AIs can't produce these outputs.

**"I need to chat with my own documents and get cited answers."**
→ **NotebookLM** for building a private knowledge base with full source attribution.

**"I need complex reasoning — maths, logic, multi-step coding."**
→ **o4** (ChatGPT Plus) or **Claude with Extended Thinking** — reasoning models that think before responding.

## The Master Routing Table

| Task | Primary tool | Why | Free alternative |
|------|-------------|-----|------------------|
| Writing, drafting, editing | Claude | Best instruction-following | Claude free tier |
| Research with sources | Perplexity | Cited, verifiable answers | Perplexity free tier |
| Comprehensive research report | Perplexity Deep Research | 15-30 automated searches | Perplexity free (daily limit) |
| Data analysis with code | ChatGPT + Code Interpreter | Executes real Python | n/a (paid feature) |
| Complex math/logic | ChatGPT o4 or Claude Extended Thinking | Reasoning models | o4-mini (ChatGPT free with limits) |
| Image generation | Bing Image Creator → Midjourney | Free first, paid for quality | Bing Image Creator (DALL-E 3) |
| Voice / narration | ElevenLabs | Best speech synthesis | ElevenLabs free (10K chars/month) |
| Music for video/content | Suno | Fastest, generous free tier | Suno free |
| Short video clip | Runway Gen-4 | Reliable free tier | Runway free tier |
| Working in Gmail/Docs | Gemini | Native Google integration | Gemini free tier |
| Working in Outlook/Teams | Microsoft 365 Copilot | Native M365 integration | Copilot.microsoft.com (free) |
| Reading a web page | Copilot in Edge | Page-aware, no copy-paste | Free (comes with Edge) |
| Very long documents (>200K tokens) | Gemini 2.5 Pro | 1M token context window | n/a |
| Private knowledge base | NotebookLM | Source-grounded, no hallucination | NotebookLM free |
| Academic research | Elicit + Consensus + Scite | Scientific literature specific | Elicit free tier |

## Multi-Tool Stacks for Different Budgets

You don't need to pay for everything. Here are practical stacks at different investment levels:

**£0 / month — Free tools only:**
- Claude free tier (Sonnet 4.6, daily message limits)
- Perplexity free (Pro Search with daily limits)
- Bing Image Creator (DALL-E 3, free in Edge)
- NotebookLM (free)
- Gemini free tier (2.5 Flash, live search)
- Copilot in Edge (free with Windows)
- Suno free, ElevenLabs free, Otter.ai free

This free stack covers 80% of what most users need. The limitations are: message limits, slower models, occasional unavailability during peak usage.

**~£20 / month — Single paid subscription:**
- **Claude Pro (£18/month):** Best choice if you primarily write, analyse, or code. Unlimited Sonnet 4.6, access to Opus, Projects, extended context, 5x faster than free tier.
- **ChatGPT Plus (£20/month):** Best choice if you heavily use Code Interpreter, DALL-E, or voice mode, or if your work is in the Microsoft ecosystem.
- **Perplexity Pro (£17/month):** Best choice if research is your primary use case — unlimited Deep Research.

**~£40 / month — Optimal dual stack (most professional users):**
- Claude Pro + free Gemini + free Perplexity + free Copilot in Edge + free NotebookLM
- Or: Claude Pro + ChatGPT Plus with both at £20 each
- This covers: best writing AI (Claude) + best data analysis (ChatGPT) + live search (Perplexity/Gemini) + knowledge base (NotebookLM)

**Enterprise (paid by employer):**
- Microsoft 365 Copilot (~£25-30/user/month as add-on)
- Google Workspace + Gemini
- Your organisation may already pay for these — check before subscribing personally

## How to Evaluate a New AI Tool

New AI tools launch every week. Here's a framework for deciding whether to add something new to your stack:

**Step 1 — Does it solve a specific problem you actually have?**
Tool novelty is not a reason to use it. Before adding anything, ask: does this do something that none of my current tools do well? If the answer is "it's a bit better at X," X needs to matter enough to justify the friction of learning a new tool.

**Step 2 — What category is it?**
Most new AI tools fit an existing category (image generation, coding assistant, writing assistant, research). Identify the category and compare it to the incumbent. Does it clearly beat the category leader? Does it offer a specific feature the leader lacks?

**Step 3 — What does it cost and what are the limits?**
Free tiers are often generous enough to evaluate. Try the free tier first. Only pay if you hit the limits doing real work you care about.

**Step 4 — Run your benchmark tasks.**
Create a small set of tasks that represent your real use cases. Run these in the new tool and compare to what you'd get from your current stack. Benchmarks from your actual work are more reliable than published capability comparisons.

**Step 5 — Is it additive or substitutive?**
Will this replace something in your current stack (substitutive, good — fewer tools to manage) or add to it (additive — only worth it if the incremental value is high)?

sections.title: Build Your Personal AI Toolkit Document
sections.content:
This is a synthesis and planning workshop. You're building a reference document that reflects your actual current workflow — not an idealised one.

**Step 1 — Create the file**
Open VS Code or Notepad. Create `my-ai-toolkit.md`.

**Step 2 — Fill in your routing table**
Start from the master routing table above and edit every row based on your own experience from lessons 2-1 through 2-7. Override any row where you have a different preference:

```markdown
# My AI Toolkit — Personal Routing Guide
Last updated: [date]

## Task routing
| Task | My primary tool | Why | My backup |
|------|----------------|-----|----------|
| Writing and drafting | | | |
| Research with sources | | | |
| Data analysis | | | |
| Images | | | |
| Working in [your email client] | | | |
| Learning a new topic | | | |
| Meeting summaries | | | |
| [Add your top 3 most common tasks] | | | |

## Current stack
- [List the tools you currently have access to]
- [Note which are paid vs. free]

## What I still want to try
- [Tools from this course you haven't tried yet]

## My evaluation criteria for new tools
1. Does it solve a specific problem I actually have?
2. Does it beat my current tool for that specific task?
3. [Add your own criteria]
```

**Step 3 — Add your real tasks**
Think about the 5 most common tasks you'd use AI for in your real work. Add them as rows. Be specific — not "writing" but "writing status update emails" or "drafting technical documentation."

**Step 4 — Budget decision**
Based on the multi-tool stacks above, write one paragraph: what is your current AI spending, and is there a different allocation that would give you more value? This might be £0 (free tools only are sufficient) or a specific paid upgrade you've decided to make.

**Save this file.** It's your living reference — update it as your stack evolves through the course.

sections.question: You need to quickly check 3 specific statistics for a report you're writing today — current inflation figures, latest unemployment data, and recent GDP growth. You need the numbers to be accurate and citable. What is the fastest, most reliable approach?
options: Ask Claude — it has comprehensive economic data from training
Ask ChatGPT — it has better factual accuracy than Claude
Use Perplexity — it searches live sources and provides cited statistics you can verify and reference
Use Gemini — Google has the best economic data
sections.explanation: For current statistics that you need to cite, Perplexity is the right tool. Economic data changes frequently — training data cutoffs mean Claude and ChatGPT may have outdated figures. Perplexity runs a live search and returns statistics with numbered citations from government sources, central banks, and authoritative organisations. You can click each citation to verify the exact figure and source before including it in your report. This is the exact use case Perplexity was built for.

sections.title: Workshop A — Head-to-Head Tool Comparison Drill
sections.content:
The fastest way to build routing instincts is to run the same task in two different tools and directly compare. This drill takes one real task from your week and tests it in two tools.

1. Pick a real writing or analysis task you need to do this week. It should be something you can complete in 5-10 minutes: a short email draft, a paragraph of explanation for a colleague, a summary of a document, or an answer to a work question.

2. Open Claude.ai in one tab and ChatGPT (chatgpt.com) in another tab, side by side.

3. Write the same prompt in both tools. Be specific and identical — copy-paste the exact same text. Do not reveal which tool you are in to yourself while reading the results.

4. Read both outputs without looking at which tool produced which. On a piece of paper, note: which response is more accurate? Which is better written? Which is more useful for the actual task? Which would require less editing?

5. Now decide: which tool won for this specific task type? Note it in your routing table.

6. Repeat with a second task type — this time pick something research-oriented or fact-dependent. Run it in Claude and in Perplexity. Compare: did Perplexity's citations change which answer you trusted more?

7. AI-check: Take one of the outputs from step 4. Paste it into the other tool and ask: *"What is missing or weak in this response? What would make it more useful?"* Note whether the AI critique is fair.

8. Update your personal toolkit document with specific routing decisions based on what you just tested — not based on what this lesson claims, but on what you actually experienced.

sections.title: Workshop B — Build Your Real AI Decision Playbook
sections.content:
You will create a practical one-page decision playbook specific to your actual job role — something you can refer to whenever you are unsure which tool to use. This is not the generic routing table from the lesson; it is your personalised version.

1. **Open a new document** called `ai-playbook-[your-name].md`. This is a document you will actually use and update.

2. **List your top 8 most frequent work tasks** — the things you do every week without fail. Be specific. Examples: "write weekly status update email", "prepare slide deck for client meeting", "research competitor pricing", "summarise long reports before presenting them", "respond to customer escalation emails".

3. **For each task, fill in these columns:**
   - Task name (specific)
   - Current approach (how you do it now, with or without AI)
   - Best AI tool for this task (from the routing table or your own experience)
   - Specific prompt template or starting approach
   - Time saved estimate (rough minutes per week)

4. **Write your prompt templates.** For your 3 highest-frequency tasks, write a reusable prompt template — a starting point you can paste and customise each time. Example for status update email: *"Write a professional status update email for [project name]. This week's progress: [fill in]. Blockers: [fill in]. Next steps: [fill in]. Audience: [manager/team]. Tone: concise and factual."*

5. **Add a new tool evaluation checklist** at the bottom of your document with these 5 questions (personalised from the lesson):
   - Does it solve a specific problem I have in my current top-8 tasks?
   - Does it beat my current tool for that task in a direct test?
   - Is the free tier sufficient for my usage level?
   - Does it require me to leave my primary workflow?
   - Does it add to or replace something already in my stack?

6. **Estimate your total AI time savings per week** by adding up the estimates from step 3. Even rough estimates help you see the aggregate value of your stack.

7. **Identify one gap.** Is there a task in your top 8 where you have no good AI tool yet? Note it as a gap to address in future lessons.

8. **AI REVIEW step:** Paste your entire playbook into Claude.ai. Send this prompt: *"Don't validate this — find 3 specific problems or gaps in my AI tool playbook. What am I missing, what's incorrectly routed, and what important use case have I overlooked for my described work context?"* Fix at least one gap based on the response.

9. **Save and date the document.** Set a calendar reminder to update it in 4 weeks after you've used these tools in your actual work.

10. **Keep this document.** It is your most important output from Part 2 of this course — a living reference that grows with your experience.

sections.title: Workshop C — AI Review of Your Current Tool Choices
sections.content:
Take an honest look at how you currently use (or avoid) AI tools in your work, and run adversarial review on your own assumptions.

1. Open a blank document. List every AI tool you have used in the past month — even casually. Next to each, note: what you used it for, roughly how often, and whether you felt the output was good enough to use without heavy editing.

2. Open Claude.ai. Paste your list and send this prompt: *"I am reviewing my current AI tool usage. Based on this list, what routing mistakes am I probably making? Where am I using tools for tasks they are not best suited for? What tools am I likely underusing given my described tasks?"*

3. Read the analysis. Identify the 1-2 suggestions that feel most accurate based on your real experience.

4. Now test the suggestion: if Claude suggests you should be using Perplexity for something you currently use Claude for, run a real task through Perplexity right now. Does it actually perform better for that task?

5. Write one paragraph in your notes: *"Based on this review, I am going to change [specific behaviour] from [current approach] to [new approach] because [specific reason from the comparison]."*

6. If you found that a tool you thought was best is not actually best for one of your tasks, update your routing table accordingly. Real experience beats any recommendation from a lesson.

sections.title: Workshop D — Evaluate a New AI Tool Against Your Stack
sections.content:
Apply the 5-step evaluation framework from this lesson to a real new AI tool — one you have heard about but not seriously tested yet.

1. **Choose a candidate tool** you are curious about. Some options if nothing comes to mind: Perplexity (if you have only used Claude), NotebookLM (if you have not tried it), Gemini (if you primarily use ChatGPT), or any tool you have seen mentioned in the past month.

2. **Run step 1 of the evaluation framework:** Write one sentence answering — does this tool solve a specific problem you have? Name the problem precisely. If you cannot name a specific problem, reconsider whether you should evaluate this tool at all.

3. **Identify the category** of the new tool. Which row(s) in the master routing table does it compete with?

4. **Set up your benchmark tasks.** Write 3 specific tasks you will run through this tool — tasks drawn from your actual work, not generic tests. Write the exact prompts you will use before opening the tool.

5. **Evaluate the free tier.** Open the tool, run your 3 benchmark tasks, and note the results. Do not pay anything yet.

6. **Score it on each dimension** from 1-5: output quality, speed, ease of use, fit for your workflow, uniqueness (does it do something your current stack cannot?).

7. **Make the substitutive vs. additive decision:** Would this replace something in your current stack, or add to it? If it adds without replacing, what is the concrete value above your current tools?

8. **Write your verdict:** one paragraph stating whether you will add this tool, why, and at what tier (free/paid). If you decide not to add it, state why specifically.

sections.question: A colleague shares an article about a new AI tool that 'beats GPT-4o on every benchmark.' They suggest your team should switch to it immediately. What is the most appropriate first response?
options: Agree to switch immediately — benchmark superiority means it will be better for all tasks
Dismiss it — established tools like Claude and ChatGPT are always more reliable than newcomers
Apply the evaluation framework: identify which specific tasks it would solve better, run it on your actual benchmark tasks, and compare before deciding
Wait 6 months — all new AI tools are unstable and should not be used professionally
sections.explanation: Benchmark scores measure performance on standardised tests, not on your specific tasks in your specific context. The evaluation framework exists exactly for this situation: identify whether the new tool solves a real problem you have, run it on tasks drawn from your actual work, and compare against your current stack. A tool that wins on benchmarks may still lose on your particular use case, or may add complexity without replacing anything. Neither immediate adoption nor blanket dismissal is the right response.

sections.question: You are working inside Microsoft Word drafting a proposal, and you want AI help to improve a section. What is the lowest-friction way to get AI assistance without leaving your document?
options: Copy the section, open a new browser tab, navigate to Claude.ai, paste the text, get the response, and copy it back
Use Microsoft 365 Copilot directly inside Word — highlight the section, click Copilot, and choose Rewrite or ask a specific question
Email the document to yourself and open it on your phone to use a mobile AI app
Save the document as a PDF and upload it to ChatGPT
sections.explanation: The routing principle 'the right tool is often the one you don't have to leave your workflow to use' applies directly here. If you have Microsoft 365 Copilot, it is already inside Word — no tab switching, no copy-pasting, no context loss. Rewriting a section takes two clicks. The Claude.ai approach (A) works but adds 5+ steps and breaks your concentration. This is why native integrations like M365 Copilot have high practical value even when standalone AI tools might have higher raw capability.

sections.content: **You've completed Part 2.** You now have a toolkit of 10+ AI tools with a principled routing framework for choosing between them. You also have a personal toolkit document that reflects your actual needs and preferences. Part 3 shifts the focus from *which tool* to *how to talk to it* — the craft of prompting that makes every tool dramatically more powerful.
